strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and emerging bottleneck in modern video generation: the latency of VAE decoders, which becomes prominent as DiT models are optimized.

The proposed method is theoretically grounded (e.g., SVD analysis for channel redundancy) and structurally sound (using topology-preserving shortcut injections to resolve residual block continuity issues during pruning).

Provides a comprehensive and rigorous evaluation on state-of-the-art VAE backbones (Wan 2.1 and LTX-Video) across multiple benchmarks (UCF-101, DAVIS 2019, VBench-2.0) and in real generation pipelines (Self-Forcing, FastVideo).

Achieves impressive speedups (up to ~6x for the decoder) with minimal loss in reconstruction quality and temporal consistency, significantly outperforming competitive baselines like Turbo-VAED and LightVAE.
weaknesses: The training pipeline is somewhat complex, involving a three-phase dynamic distillation process that requires substantial training computation (approximately 300 GPU-hours).

The operator configuration and pruning ratio choices (e.g., choosing which blocks to swap with 2D convs or 3D DW convs and applying 1/8 vs 1/4 pruning ratios) are somewhat heuristic and customized manually for each model (Wan vs LTX-Video) rather than being determined via an automated search framework.
The latent space visualization in Figure 10 is brief and lacks details in the main text regarding how the samples were projected and evaluated.

strengths: Addresses a timely and highly practical bottleneck in modern video generative models: as the DiT models are accelerated, VAE decoding emerges as the new dominant latency bottleneck.
Well-motivated design choices based on thorough analyses, such as SVD analysis to demonstrate channel redundancy and block-wise latency breakdown showing CausalConv3D as the primary bottleneck.

Innovative technical solutions, particularly the independence-aware channel pruning with topology-preserving shortcut injection initialized via least-squares mapping, which beautifully handles channel mismatch across residual blocks.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation across multiple video VAEs (Wan 2.1, LTX-Video, HunyuanVideo, CogVideoX), hardware platforms (high-end GPU and edge device), and downstream generation frameworks (Self-Forcing, FastVideo).
Excellent presentation, clear writing, and highly detailed supplementary material including generalization studies on DAVIS 2019 and VRAM usage analysis.
weaknesses: The placement of operators (depthwise separable vs. 2D convolutions) and the selection of pruning ratios seem to require manual, heuristic tuning for each specific VAE architecture (as shown in the different configurations for Wan 2.1 and LTX-Video).
The training pipeline is somewhat complex and multi-staged, requiring three separate distillation phases and approximately 300 GPU-hours of training on high-end GPUs, which limits rapid iteration.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly critical and timely bottleneck in modern video generation: the latency of VAE decoders, which becomes the primary computational bottleneck as diffusion transformer (DiT) modules are accelerated.

The proposed method is technically sound, utilizing SVD analysis to justify channel pruning, and introduces a clever topology-preserving shortcut injection using least-squares projection to maintain residual block connectivity.

The stage-wise operator optimization represents a sensible design choice, replacing computationally heavy 3D causal convolutions with 3D depthwise separable convolutions in deep layers and 2D convolutions in shallow layers.

The paper features extremely thorough experiments, demonstrating substantial speedups (~6×) on both consumer GPUs (RTX 5090D) and edge devices (Jetson Orin) while preserving high reconstruction quality.

Excellent generalization and integration testing are provided, evaluating the compressed decoders on multiple generation frameworks (Self-Forcing, FastVideo, Causal Forcing), high-resolution datasets (DAVIS 2019 at 720p), and alternative backbones (HunyuanVideo, CogVideoX).
weaknesses: The core compression techniques—such as linear reconstruction for channel pruning (similar to ThiNet) and depthwise separable convolutions—are relatively standard. The novelty lies primarily in their specific integration, training initialization, and adaptation to video VAEs.

While the compressed VAE decoders are 'plug-and-play' for the downstream DiT models (requiring no DiT fine-tuning), the compression process itself requires a non-trivial training overhead (300 GPU-hours on 4× A5880 GPUs) for each unique VAE architecture.

Although the speedups are substantial, there is still a noticeable drop in reconstruction metrics (e.g., a drop of ~2.8 dB PSNR on Wan 2.1), which might compromise high-frequency visual details or text rendering in extremely fine-grained generation tasks.

Some of the visual figures are slightly cluttered and hard to parse. For instance, the text and speedup labels within Figure 1 and the latency breakdown charts in Figure 7 would benefit from larger fonts and clearer layout organization.
